What the differences mean

Dealectric does not test units. Every figure here comes from the maker's page, Apple's spec pages or a named publication, as listed under sources. Prices were read on 18 November 2026. All six rows were at or under $300 at the maker's store that day.

  • FOPO S1, both screens running: 2 × (1920 × 1080) = 4,147,200 added pixels. On a laptop that drives one external display, only 1 × 2,073,600 pixels light, because each screen needs its own connection.
  • Duex Float 2 Pro through one connection: 2560 × 1600 = 4,096,000 pixels. That is 98.8% of the S1's two-screen total (4,096,000 ÷ 4,147,200), using one video output.
  • Weight: the S1 is 1.42 kg × 2.2046 = 3.13 lb, or 1.57 lb per added screen. itechguides lists the Float 2 Pro at 2.9 lb, which is 0.23 lb lighter for nearly the same pixel count.
  • Brightness ratings make a weak tiebreaker. Notebookcheck measured 193.1 cd/m² at most on FOPO's 2022 12-inch triple extender with an X-Rite i1Pro 2. That is an older model, so it isn't a figure for any screen above. Still, it suggests 250 versus 300 rated nits is a thin reason to choose one screen over another.

How many extender screens your laptop can light

FOPO states the rule plainly for the S1: "Two displays. Two video connections. Each S1 screen needs its own supported video connection." No driver is involved, so the laptop itself has to drive both screens. FOPO adds that charging-only USB-C ports cannot carry video. On a laptop with one video-capable USB-C port and an HDMI port, the second screen can run from HDMI with a separate USB-A cable for power.

Apple's spec pages give the limit for each Mac:

  • MacBook Air M1 and M2: one external display.
  • 13-inch MacBook Air M3 and base 14-inch MacBook Pro M3: one external display with the lid open. A second works only with the lid closed, and you can't close the lid with an extender clipped to it.
  • MacBook Air M4 and current M5: up to two external displays with the built-in screen on.

A single-cable hub won't get around the one-display limit. Plugable, a dock maker, states that "MST is not supported on macOS for extended displays": screens on one MST cable mirror instead of extending. On those Macs, three working screens need a driver-based extender, and the one we list, the FOPO S788, costs {price:fopo-s788-16-inch-triple-laptop-screen-extender}, over this budget. On Windows, count the USB-C ports that carry video (DisplayPort Alt Mode) plus any HDMI port.

If your laptop qualifies for two screens, {buy:fopo-s1-dual-14-inch-laptop-screen-extender} is the two-screen extender under $300 that we link. If you have a 15–16-inch laptop with one video output, {buy:mobile-pixels-duex-float-2-pro} adds nearly as many pixels on one cable.

Where we drew the line:

  • Over $300: the Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro ({price:mobile-pixels-trio-3-pro}), the FOPO S11 and the FOPO S788.
  • Duex Plus DS: the 13.3-inch version of the Duex Max DS, $159.99 at Mobile Pixels, for 13–14-inch laptops by itechguides' account.
  • UPERFECT 14-inch dual and 2K swivel extenders: left out because UPERFECT's US store doesn't list them, so we had no maker page for their video path.
  • Teamgee: its attachable single screens start at $199.99 on Teamgee's store.

Not recommended

A driver-free two-screen extender for a base M1, M2 or M3 MacBook Air. Apple's limit of one external display with the lid open means you pay for two screens and light one. On those Macs the Duex Max DS gives the same single screen without the extra weight.
